name: Femur vs tibia lengthening

card.summary: The choice of which leg bone to lengthen: femur gets the larger, better-documented gains, tibia is usually staged later and carries its own nerve and ankle risks.
card.aka: Thigh vs shin lengthening; femoral vs tibial lengthening
card.note: Evidence comes mostly from reconstructive and dwarfism series; cosmetic-only data are sparse and surgeon-reported.

quick.overview:
Cosmetic leg lengthening in the looksmaxxing community is usually discussed as a choice between lengthening the femur (thigh bone), the tibia (shin bone), or both in stages. Forum users commonly describe the femur as the segment that yields more length and is done first, with the tibia added later for extra height.

Published literature on limb lengthening comes mainly from treatment of leg-length differences, trauma and skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia. It describes complications in both segments, but studies specifically comparing femur and tibia for purely cosmetic height gain are scarce.
quick.mechanism: Both procedures cut the bone and then separate the ends gradually so new bone forms in the gap (distraction osteogenesis), using either an external frame or a motorised nail placed inside the bone marrow canal. The femur is surrounded by large muscles, whereas the tibia sits just under the skin with nerves and vessels running close to the ankle and foot.
quick.risks: Reported complications in limb lengthening in general include nerve injury, joint stiffness or contracture, delayed or failed bone healing, infection, and hardware problems. Descriptions in the literature associate femoral lengthening with knee stiffness and quadriceps tightness, and tibial lengthening with ankle and nerve-related problems. The procedure is elective in the cosmetic context and is generally not covered by insurance.

chain: Surgeon cuts the femur, tibia or both and slowly separates the ends
New bone forms in the gap, adding length to the leg
Overall height rises by several centimetres once healing finishes
angle.text: Limb lengthening adds permanent height by lengthening the thigh bone, shin bone or both, and the choice of segment shapes how many centimetres can be added and which structures are stressed. Forum plans often stage the femur first and the tibia later.

lead: Femur vs tibia lengthening refers, in looksmaxxing and limb-lengthening communities, to the decision about which leg bone to lengthen surgically to add height: the femur (thigh bone), the tibia (shin bone), or both, usually in stages. Both operations use distraction osteogenesis, in which a bone is cut and the ends are slowly pulled apart, at a rate commonly given as about 1 mm per day, so that new bone forms in the gap [1]. The result is a permanent gain in leg length and, with it, standing height and leg proportions.

Gavriil Ilizarov's work in Kurgan, Russia, from the 1950s made the technique practical, and cosmetic lengthening for height developed in several countries from the late twentieth century [1][13]. Forum participants often describe the femur as the first-choice segment because it is said to allow more length per surgery and to be better tolerated, with tibial lengthening added later by those who want more height. A Grokipedia summary reports typical cosmetic gains of roughly 6 to 8 cm for the femur and 4 to 6 cm for the tibia per stage, about 10 to 13 cm for a staged total, and notes that surgeons are described as more conservative with the tibia [2]; these figures vary between sources.

Published clinical research on lengthening comes largely from reconstructive orthopaedics and skeletal dysplasia, where femur and tibia are lengthened for medical reasons [3][4]. Studies comparing the two segments for purely cosmetic height gain are limited, so statements about relative risk in the cosmetic setting rest largely on surgeon experience and case series.

paras: Lengthening adds height by lengthening one or both leg segments. The femur runs from hip to knee and is typically about 40 to 50 cm in adults, while the tibia runs from knee to ankle at around 35 to 40 cm, according to a Grokipedia summary [2]. Because the femur is wrapped in large muscle and the tibia lies close under the skin, the two segments differ in the soft tissue that has to stretch with the bone and in the nerves and vessels nearby.

People pursuing cosmetic lengthening describe the aims as greater height, proportionally longer legs, and the social and professional benefits they associate with height. Reported benefits in patient accounts summarised from Reddit's limb-lengthening community include higher confidence, less teasing about height and perceived better dating or career prospects, though the same summary stresses that these accounts are individual and variable [2].

Bernhard von Langenbeck proposed bone lengthening in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical series in 1905, cutting the femur and applying traction through a heel pin in 26 people with malformed legs; infection, tissue death and non-union were common and the method was not adopted [1]. Grokipedia also credits Vittorio Putti with a 1921 paper on femoral lengthening with external fixators and springs [2].

Gavriil Ilizarov began studying the method in the 1950s in Kurgan and, per Wikipedia, treated over 15,000 people; he developed ring external fixators and determined suitable separation rates [1]. His discovery of distraction osteogenesis came when he lengthened rather than shortened an adjustable frame and saw callus form [13]. The apparatus reached US medicine in 1987, and later developments included the Taylor Spatial Frame [13]. Dror Paley is credited in Grokipedia with helping bring the Ilizarov method to North America in the 1980s [2].

Internal lengthening devices followed: the motorised Fitbone nail from Wittenstein is described as offering accurate correction and lower infection risk than mechanical systems [1], and magnetically controlled nails such as PRECICE were studied in post-market registrations beginning in 2012 [7][8]. Grokipedia dates FDA approval of PRECICE to 2011, notes that its EU certificate was suspended in April 2021 over quality concerns, and reports a 2023 US clearance of an updated system [2].

In distraction osteogenesis the surgeon cuts the bone (osteotomy), waits a latency period of about a week, separates the ends gradually, and then allows a consolidation period while the new bone hardens. Reviews describe a distraction rate of about 1 mm per day; separating too quickly is associated with failure of new bone to form, and too slowly with premature union [1].

Methods range from frames worn on the outside of the leg to combined and fully internal approaches. A comparative study of femoral lengthening reported that lengthening over a nail had fewer complications than an earlier internal kinetic-distraction device [5]. A study of children found that adding a flexible intramedullary nail to Ilizarov fixation changed the healing index compared with the frame alone [3]. Motorised internal nails, including magnetically controlled retrograde femoral nails, have been described in the medical literature [6].

An Ilizarov-style frame is a modular external fixator of rings fixed to the bone with wires and pins, adjusted several times a day, which allows early weight-bearing [13]. Wikipedia notes that lengthening a leg bone may also require lengthening the Achilles tendon, and that inflammation, muscle transfixion by pins and joint contracture are recognised problems [13].

Grokipedia's summary of recovery describes a hospital stay of a few days, distraction of roughly 10 days per centimetre, consolidation of about 4 to 6 months for a 6 to 8 cm gain, full weight-bearing at 2 to 3 months, and 1 to 2 years to full activity, with nail removal 12 to 18 months after surgery [2]. Individual courses vary.

Online summaries describe the femur as the segment that tolerates the most lengthening, with cosmetic targets of about 6 to 8 cm per stage and with fewer complications than tibial lengthening [2]. Orthopaedic papers describe knee stiffness and quadriceps tightness as recognised problems; a case series describes a limited quadricepsplasty used to treat contracture that developed during femoral lengthening [9]. Lengthening over a nail in the femur had fewer complications than an internal kinetic device in a comparative study [5].

The same summary describes tibial targets as more modest, around 4 to 6 cm, and says the tibia carries higher risk to the ankle and knee [2]. Staged plans are described in which the femurs are done first and the tibias at least 12 months later, with total gains above about 13 to 15 cm said to raise complication rates sharply [2]. Animal research has shown that denervation impairs bone regeneration in rabbit tibial lengthening, which points to the importance of intact nerve supply to the healing segment [10]. A case report describes a pseudoaneurysm after high tibial osteotomy and limb lengthening [12].

Simultaneous lengthening of both femurs and tibias has been studied in people with achondroplasia, including a registered trial that started in 2002 with 22 patients [11]. A review of limb lengthening in achondroplasia describes substantial complication rates and notes that guidelines on timing, sequence and extent are not uniform around the world [4]. These populations differ from cosmetic patients in age, indication and bone quality.

Cosmetic limb lengthening has been marketed in India, where demand is described as high and the industry as unregulated; patients as young as 13 or 14 have been reported, with outcomes that included infections, further surgery and less height than expected, and some said surgeons had misled them about risks [1]. One Indian surgeon quoted by Wikipedia criticised the lack of training; China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects [1]. Wikipedia also notes the 1997 film Gattaca depicts leg lengthening within an identity-concealment plot [1].

Grokipedia lists Turkey and India among medical-tourism destinations and says the International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery warns against unlicensed clinics abroad [2]. On height-focused forums, the femur-first, tibia-later plan is a frequent topic, and members compare surgeon techniques, internal nails versus external frames, and recovery experience, often timing surgery around school or work breaks [2].

The Grokipedia summary reports, from one series of 814 procedures, nerve injury in about 9 percent of limbs, joint stiffness in up to about 5 percent of segments, nonunion in about 5 percent of intramedullary segments, reoperation in about 15 percent with nails, and higher rates at one specialist centre for cosmetic patients [2]. Because that source is AI-generated and its figures are internally inconsistent in places, they are indicative rather than definitive.

More generally, the literature on distraction osteogenesis lists infection, hardware failure, healing problems and nerve injury among recognised complications [1]. Wikipedia gives figures from mixed medical series: infection in about 5 percent overall, bone not growing in the desired direction in 7 to 9 percent, hardware failure in 3 to 4.5 percent, and failure to follow the distraction protocol in 4.5 percent; these are not specific to femur or tibia [1]. A 2023 FDA notice reiterated limits on use of one magnetic nail system in small or heavy patients, per Grokipedia [2].

No clinical studies were found that directly compare femur against tibia lengthening for cosmetic height gain in healthy adults. Related human research covers limb lengthening for leg length discrepancy, trauma and achondroplasia, including a comparison of lengthening techniques in the femur [5], a series on achondroplasia [4], and registered trials of simultaneous femoral and tibial lengthening [11] and of a magnetic intramedullary lengthening system [7][8].

lore.intro: On height-focused forums and the limb-lengthening subreddit the femur-or-tibia question is treated as a core planning decision, framed as a trade-off between amount of height gained and risk to nerves and the ankle.

claims.claim: The femur gives more height with fewer complications, so it should come first.
claims.believers: Community members describe femoral lengthening as the main route to height and the tibia as an optional second stage [2].
claims.experts: A summary of the literature reports femoral lengthening as having fewer complications than tibial and tibial targets as more conservative [2]. A study of femoral techniques found complication differences between methods [5].

claims.claim: Tibial lengthening carries more risk to nerves and the ankle.
claims.believers: Proponents of femur-only plans cite nerve and ankle problems as reasons to avoid or delay the tibia [2].
claims.experts: One summary reports nerve injury in a minority of limbs and higher ankle and knee risk with the tibia [2]; denervation impaired bone regeneration in a rabbit tibial lengthening model [10]. No trial has compared the two in cosmetic patients.

claims.claim: Both bones can be lengthened together for a larger total gain.
claims.believers: Users describe four-bone staged plans as the way to reach the largest cosmetic total, with a 10 to 13 cm range cited [2].
claims.experts: Simultaneous lengthening of femurs and tibias has been studied in achondroplasia [11][4], not in cosmetic patients.

claims.claim: Internal nails are better than external frames because they avoid pin sites and a frame.
claims.believers: Internal nail users describe easier daily life and fewer pin-site infections [2].
claims.experts: A comparative femoral study found lengthening over a nail had fewer complications than an older internal device [5]; Wikipedia describes Fitbone as offering lower infection risk than mechanical systems [1].

claims.claim: Surgery abroad is a practical lower-cost route.
claims.believers: Forum discussion lists Turkey and India among destinations with all-inclusive packages [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia records reports from India of infections, reoperation and less height than expected [1]; a professional society warns against unlicensed clinics abroad [2].

claims.claim: A gain above roughly 13 to 15 cm is the practical ceiling.
claims.believers: Forum plans treat this as the limit set by bone and soft tissue tolerance [2].
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports complications rising sharply beyond that range, though sources differ [2].
